name: Wrought-Leviathan
geological_features: Planet-spanning hurricane in the equatorial belt
Metallic hydrogen ocean beneath the cloud layer
Orbital debris ring of captured asteroids
Perpetual storm systems with lightning discharges visible from orbit
specific_features: Research outpost on the largest moon
Signal of unknown origin from deep within the atmosphere
description: Wrought-Leviathan dominates its star system with the gravitational authority of a body nearly as large as some failed stars, its banded atmosphere a churning canvas of amber, bronze, and deep copper that suggests a world forged rather than formed. A permanent hurricane three times the diameter of most habitable worlds rotates in the equatorial belt, its eye a window into deeper atmospheric layers that glow with the pressure-generated heat of the interior. Rings of captured asteroids encircle the planet, their surfaces polished to metallic brightness by the gas giant's intense radiation belt.

Observing Wrought-Leviathan from its largest moon is an experience that redefines one's sense of scale. The planet fills half the sky, its cloud formations moving with a ponderous grace that belies the thousand-kilometer-per-hour winds driving them. Lightning storms visible from orbit illuminate the cloud deck in sheets of blue-white light, and the radiation belt creates auroras at the poles that dwarf any terrestrial comparison, curtains of light that extend millions of kilometers into space.

Atmospheric probes have detected living organisms within the cloud layers: vast, gas-bag creatures that float on thermal updrafts and filter atmospheric compounds for sustenance. These organisms, some measuring kilometers across, were initially mistaken for weather formations before their purposeful movement patterns betrayed their biological nature. A persistent signal from deep within the planet's metallic hydrogen layer has resisted all analysis, its complexity suggesting either an unknown natural process or something deliberate at the bottom of an atmosphere no probe has survived to reach.

Wrought-Leviathan's helium-3 reserves are effectively limitless, but atmospheric mining operations must contend with the crushing gravity, extreme wind speeds, and the living inhabitants of the cloud layer whose ecological role is poorly understood. The signal from the deep atmosphere has spawned theories ranging from the mundane to the fantastical, and the most recent deep-dive probe recorded structures in the metallic hydrogen layer that appeared manufactured before contact was lost. The research outpost on the largest moon continues its vigil, watching and listening to a world that may be more than it appears.
